strengths: Resolves multiple significant open problems in the computational and parameterized complexity of neural network verification and zonotope containment, including questions explicitly posed at COLT 2025.

Provides tight computational complexity characterizations: establishes that naive enumeration algorithms with runtime $n^{(\ell-1)d} \cdot \text{poly}(N)$ are essentially optimal under the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH).

The core technical reductions are elegant and mathematically rigorous, notably the use of Sidon sets to compress the input dimension linearly with clique size in the Multicolored Clique reduction, and the homogenization gadget that preserves bias-free properties without adding layer depth.

The paper is very thorough and broad in scope, addressing exact computation, inapproximability, injectivity, surjectivity, and both dimension $d$ and depth $\ell$ parameterizations, as well as positive algorithmic results for input-convex neural networks (ICNNs) and randomized approximation via subspace embeddings.
The manuscript is clearly written and well-structured, with helpful intuitive explanations and geometric figures illustrating the reduction gadgets.
weaknesses: A complexity gap remains between the lower bound ($W[\ell-1]$-hardness) and the algorithmic upper bounds (containment in $W[P]$ for 2 layers, and XP in general), leaving open whether these problems are complete for any specific level of the $W$-hierarchy.

The work is entirely theoretical with no empirical demonstrations; while standard for a computational complexity contribution, some discussion on whether real-world verification benchmarks align with the pessimistic ETH lower bounds would enhance practical impact.
